paths/prayer-and-mysticism-across-the-ce: Prayer and mysticism across the centuries

A journey through Christian ways of prayer and experiences of God: desert hermits and monks, the Jesus Prayer and the uncreated light, medieval mystics and their condemnations, Reformation critiques, Ignatian and Carmelite spirituality, Quakers, Moravians and Methodists, and the dawn-prayer, Pentecostal and contemplative movements of today.
Into the desert

Around 270 Antony of Egypt heard the call "go, sell what you have" and withdrew into the desert; others followed. The Desert Fathers and Mothers fought the passions with prayer, fasting and work under the guidance of elders, and Evagrius and Cassian passed their wisdom to East and West.
Benedict and the rhythm of prayer and work

Benedict’s Rule (c.530) ordered a community around the Divine Office, sacred reading and manual work. Lectio divina, later described by Guigo II as reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation, became the West’s school of prayer; Irish monks carried their own ascetic, missionary spirituality across Europe.
Light from Tabor: Eastern prayer of the heart

Symeon the New Theologian (c.1000) insisted that Christians can consciously experience the divine light. On Mount Athos, monks praying the Jesus Prayer in stillness were defended by Gregory Palamas, and councils at Constantinople upheld the hesychasts in 1341 and 1351.
Medieval mystics and a condemnation

Francis of Assisi received the stigmata at La Verna (1224); Hildegard of Bingen recorded visions; Meister Eckhart preached detachment and the birth of God in the soul until 28 of his propositions were condemned in 1329; Julian of Norwich and Catherine of Siena testified to God’s love.
The Imitation of Christ

In the Low Countries, Geert Groote’s Devotio Moderna fostered simple, methodical, Christ-centred piety among lay brothers and sisters. The Imitation of Christ, traditionally ascribed to Thomas à Kempis, became one of the most read Christian books.
Reformation: the Word, vocation and the saints

Luther and Calvin rejected monastic vows, ladders of mystical ascent and the invocation of saints, teaching prayer as faith’s response to God’s promises through Christ alone and holiness as daily vocation. Catholics and Orthodox defended asking the saints’ prayers.
Spanish masters: Ignatius, Teresa and John

Ignatius of Loyola’s experiences at Manresa became the Spiritual Exercises; Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross mapped the soul’s journey through the interior castle and the dark night. Later, Rome condemned the "quietism" of Molinos (1687), showing the Church’s caution.
Protestant heart religion

Puritans practised Scripture meditation; Quakers waited in silence for the inward light; the Moravians at Herrnhut began a hundred-year prayer watch (1727); John Wesley felt his heart "strangely warmed" (1738) and taught the means of grace.
The Philokalia and the Russian elders

The Philokalia (1782) gathered hesychast writings for all believers; Paisius Velichkovsky carried it to Russia, where Seraphim of Sarov taught the acquisition of the Holy Spirit and The Way of a Pilgrim spread the Jesus Prayer among ordinary people.
Dawn prayer, tongues and silence

Korean Christians have prayed together before dawn since the Pyongyang revival era; African prayer churches and revivals made vigils central; Pentecostals pray in tongues and for healing; Merton and Centering Prayer revived contemplative silence, provoking debate about whether such methods are biblical.

paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/summar: From the worship of the first Jewish Christians to the creeds of Nicaea and Constantinople: how the church moved from praying to Father, Son and Spirit to defining one God in three persons, and who disagreed along the way.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/steps/: Raw material: one God, worship of Jesus, the Spirit

The first Christians were Jewish monotheists who confessed the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) yet prayed to and through Jesus as Lord, and spoke of the Spirit as God's own presence. Texts such as Matthew 28:19, 2 Corinthians 13:14 and John 1:1-14 set Father, Son and Spirit side by side without yet offering a technical account of how they relate.
Apologists and the Logos

Second-century writers like Justin Martyr explained Christ as the divine Logos (Word/Reason) through whom God made and reveals the world; Irenaeus spoke of the Son and Spirit as God's 'two hands'. Their language was sometimes subordinationist by later standards, but it secured Christ's divine origin against Gnostic and Marcionite systems.
Tertullian and the threat of modalism

Against Praxeas, who taught that the Father himself was born and suffered, Tertullian coined Latin terms that would last: God is one 'substance' (substantia) in three 'persons' (personae), a 'trinity' (trinitas). Modalism, later linked with Sabellius, held that Father, Son and Spirit are successive modes of one person; it was rejected as erasing real relationships within God.
Origen and eternal generation

Origen of Alexandria taught that the Son is eternally begotten of the Father: there was never a time when the Father was without his Word. Yet he also ranked the Son and Spirit beneath the Father, so both sides of the fourth-century debate could claim his legacy.
Arius and the Council of Nicaea

The Alexandrian presbyter Arius argued that the Son, though exalted, was a creature: 'there was when he was not'. Constantine summoned the first ecumenical council, which declared the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father and anathematised Arius' slogans.
Fifty years of conflict

Nicaea did not end the dispute. Many bishops disliked homoousios as unscriptural or modalist-sounding; emperors favoured compromise formulas, and at Ariminum and Seleucia (359) a 'homoian' creed (the Son is 'like' the Father) prevailed for a time. Athanasius, exiled five times, defended Nicaea as necessary for salvation: only God can make us partakers of God.
The Cappadocians and the Spirit

Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus and Gregory of Nyssa (with their sister Macrina's influence) distinguished one ousia (being) from three hypostaseis (persons), defined by their relations: unbegotten, begotten, proceeding. Basil's On the Holy Spirit defended worshipping the Spirit with the Father and the Son against the 'Spirit-fighters' (Pneumatomachi).
Constantinople 381: the Nicene Creed completed

The second ecumenical council reaffirmed Nicaea and expanded the article on the Holy Spirit, 'the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified'. This Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed is still shared by Orthodox, Catholics, Oriental Orthodox, the Church of the East and most Protestants.
Augustine, the West and the filioque

Augustine's On the Trinity (c. 400-420) explored the Trinity through analogies of the mind and stressed the Spirit as the bond of love between Father and Son. In Spain the Third Council of Toledo (589) added that the Spirit proceeds from the Father 'and the Son' (filioque), an addition that later became a central grievance in the East-West schism.
Dissenters and modern revival

Trinitarian faith has been challenged since the Reformation by antitrinitarian movements (Socinians, Unitarians), and in the modern era by groups outside historic Nicene orthodoxy such as Jehovah's Witnesses, Latter-day Saints and Oneness Pentecostals. At the same time 20th-century theologians such as Karl Barth and Karl Rahner (whose 1967 essay argued that the 'economic' Trinity is the 'immanent' Trinity) sparked a major revival of Trinitarian theology.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/0: Who is the first known writer to use the Latin word 'trinitas' for God?
Tertullian used 'trinitas' (and 'substance' and 'persons') around 213 in Against Praxeas. The Greek 'trias' appears slightly earlier in Theophilus of Antioch (c. 180).
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/1: What key word did the Council of Nicaea (325) use to describe the Son's relation to the Father?
Nicaea declared the Son homoousios with the Father; 'homoiousios' and 'homoios' were later compromise or rival terms.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/2: Which slogan is associated with Arius?
'God became man that we might become God'
'What has not been assumed has not been healed'
Arius held that the Son had a beginning: 'there was when he was not'. The other lines come from Athanasius, Tertullian and Gregory of Nazianzus.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/3: Modalism, associated with Sabellius, taught that...
Father, Son and Spirit are three gods
Father, Son and Spirit are successive modes or masks of one person
The Spirit is a force, not a person
Modalism preserves God's oneness by treating the three as roles or modes of a single person, which critics said erased the real relationships seen in the Gospels.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/4: Which council expanded the creed's article on the Holy Spirit?
The Council of Constantinople in 381 confessed the Spirit as 'the Lord, the giver of life' who is worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/5: The Cappadocian formula for the Trinity is usually summarised as...
Basil and the Gregories distinguished the one divine being (ousia) from the three persons (hypostaseis).
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/6: Where was the filioque ('and the Son') first officially added to the creed?
The Third Council of Toledo (589) is the earliest well-known conciliar use; Rome adopted the addition in the liturgy only around 1014.
paths/how-the-trinity-was-defined/quiz/7: Which of these groups rejects the doctrine of the Trinity?
Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the Son is a created being, placing them outside historic Nicene orthodoxy; the other three affirm the Nicene Creed.
